key_insight: Chiral-interference benchmark circuits reveal that composite gates can preserve single-gate robustness while still failing at the full-circuit phase-sensitive task, so phase fidelity—not just pulse robustness—must be benchmarked.
engineering_relevance: For quantum hardware and control-stack design, these circuits provide a compact, hardware-native test that distinguishes true end-to-end gate fidelity from isolated rotation error tolerance.
method: Encoded three- and four-level chiral-resolution interference models in a two-qubit register.
Implemented enantiomer-dependent behavior using a conditional phase in the four-level circuit and a sign-flipped final rotation in the three-level circuit.
Replaced elementary single-qubit rotations with composite sequences (B5, SK1, BB1, H5s, X5) and compared output-state populations under introduced angle errors.
evidence_signal: On IBM quantum hardware, both circuits produced the expected enantiomer-dependent outputs with nearly 98% probability, and H5s/X5 kept target populations high up to about 50% relative error versus roughly 8% for elementary rotations.
watch_item: Variable-rotation composite sequences may not preserve the relative phases required by interference-based algorithms, so apparent single-gate robustness can be misleading in circuit-level deployment.
paper_title: Phase-Sensitive Benchmarking of Composite Quantum Gates with Chiral-Interference Circuits on Quantum Hardware
